newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslems-Serbs fight in refugee village.
newsitem.headline: Moslems-Serbs fight in refugee village.

text.p: Moslems and Serbs fought with mortars and small arms on Tuesday in the disputed village of Gajevi after Moslem refugees tried to re-settle it.
NATO peacekeepers accused the Bosnian government of fomenting the violence by sending the Moslems back to the village on Serb territory without prior agreement.
"We believe this to be a deliberate, orchestrated and provocative move to circumvent established procedures for the return of refugees," NATO spokesman Major Simon Haselock said.
Around 600 Moslems including women and children entered Gajevi in northeast Bosnia on Monday. The village is in the Zone of Separation (ZOS) between Serb and government controlled territory.
Male refugees who remained in the village overnight said they were forced to flee by up to 300 Serbs firing mortars, rocket propelled grenades and small arms before before fleeing.
Two Moslems were hurt, one seriously, in the three-hour attack which began at 7 a.m.
The independent Belgrade news agency Beta quoted the deputy Bosnian Serb Defence Minister Milenko Karisik as blaming the Moslems for starting the fighting.
He told Beta the refugees fired on Bosnian Serb police, injuring two, and that both sides used mortars.
Corporal Daniel Voss, a U.S. peacekeeper sent to Gajevi told reporters: "When we got there, there was some small arms fire and some mortars. There were very loud explosions."
A Reuter photographer in the area saw several hundred Moslems villagers heading for Gajevi again during the afternoon.
The ZOS is an area on either side of former front lines in Bosnia within which NATO has wide-ranging authority under the terms of the Dayton peace agreement.
Gajevi is inside the ZOS but on the Serb side of what is known as the Inter-Entity Boundary Line (IEBL), which separates Moslem-Croat and Serb-held territory in Bosnia.
The U.N. refugee agency said that none of the returnees had been approved under an internationally-supervised application process agreed by the formerly warring parties.
Shooting on Monday wounded at least one Serb.
Detachments of armed Serb police had been observed by NATO in the Gajevi area and NATO expressed strong suspicions that some Moslems in the area were armed as well.

Whoever provoked the Gajevi incident, refugee officials acknowledge the Dayton peace agreement's promise that refugees would be able to return to their homes across de facto ethnic boundary lines has not been redeemed.
Several million people were uprooted during the war, some fleeing to other safer parts of Bosnia and others taking refuge in Europe or countries further abroad.
As many as 250,000 of those refugees and displaced persons have returned voluntarily during 1996, but virtually none of them have gone home to areas controlled by rival ethnic groups.
Serb leaders, who control the 49 per cent of Bosnia known as Republika Srbska, are vociferous in their determination to maintain the "ethnically cleansed" territory they fought for.

"The ZOS is the only area in Bosnia where minorities can return because NATO has the ultimate say there, not the Bosnian Serbs, who normally oppose returns," said Kris Janowski, Sarajevo spokesman for the U.N. refugee agency.
"There is complete hostility towards returns in Republika Srpska and indeed there is no process for return to Republika Srbska since there's no cooperation by the authorities."
